overview.body:
**Gb** ​(*geb*) — ‌The Earth, ‌its Riches ​and ​its Snakes ​· Earth, ​goose ​— belongs ‌to the ​Egyptian tradition, ​where ‌it is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Earth, ‌Vegetation, Snakes". ​The name ​means ​"Earth, goose ​(Egyptian gb)"[^1].

​**Gb** — ‌Geb ​— is ‌the earth ​itself as ‌a ​god: the ‌ground that ​yields ‌gold and ​grain, the ​floor of ‌the ‌world, and ‌father of ​the third ​generation ‌of the ​gods. He ​lies ‌beneath his ​sister-wife Nut, ​parted from ‌her ​by Shu, ‌and his ​laughter is ​the ​tremor in ​the ground ‌— ‌the Egyptians ​heard earthquakes ‌as the ​earth-god ​laughing.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ‌name as ‌**Gb** ‌and serves ​its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/geb/). ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ‌— ​a description ​computed from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*geb* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/ɡɛb/ ​(conventional)** ​— ‌Conventional ​reading — ​Egyptian ‌vocalisation ​not ‌attested.[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by ​phoneme:

- **G-** ​— ​Written ​gb; ​the ‌g ​is ‌a voiced ​velar ‌stop, ​the ‌b ​a ‌voiced bilabial. ​Conventionally ​vocalised ‌“Geb”.
- ‌**-b** ‌— ​Final ​b consonantal; ‌the ​goose-determinative ​often ‌accompanies ​the ​name.

‌For the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ​approximation ​is: ‌“GHEB” — ‌one ​syllable, ‌hard ​g

​Kindred ‌and ‌historical forms ‌of ‌the ​name:

- ‌**Greek** ​— ​Κῆβ (Kêb)

​The ‌goose ​(gb) ​is ​both ‌his ​sacred animal ​and ​a ‌pun ​on ‌his ​name ‌— “the ​Cackler”. ‌The ‌name ​is ​among ​the ​shortest in ‌the ‌Egyptian ​pantheon.

domains.body:
**Gb** ​— Geb ‌— is ‌the ​earth itself ​as ​a god: ​the ground ​that ‌yields gold ​and ​grain, the ‌floor of ​the ‌world, and ​father of ‌the ​third generation ​of ​the gods. ​He lies ​beneath ‌his sister-wife ​Nut, ‌parted from ​her by ‌Shu, ​and his ‌laughter ​is the ‌tremor in ​the ​ground — ‌the Egyptians ‌heard ‌earthquakes as ​the ​earth-god laughing.[^1]

### ‌The Earth ​God

​The soil, ‌the ​mines, the ​buried treasure: ‌everything ​underfoot is ‌his body ​and ​his property.

### ​The ​Cackler

His ‌sacred goose ‌gives ​him the ‌epithet ​“the Cackler”; ​his cry ‌was ‌the world’s ‌first sound ‌in ​some cosmogonies.

### ‌Father ​of the ​Ennead

By ​Nut ‌he fathered ​Osiris, ​Isis, Seth, ​Nephthys, Horus ‌the ​Elder — ​the ​gods whose ‌quarrels drive ​Egyptian ‌myth.

### Judge ​of the ‌Divine ​Tribunal

He ‌presides ‌over the ​council of ​gods ​in the ​succession ‌myth of ‌Horus and ​Seth.

sources.citation: Contendings of Horus and Seth (New Kingdom narrative).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Gb ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Earth God** ​— ​The ​soil, ‌the ​mines, the ‌buried ​treasure: ‌everything ​underfoot ‌is his ​body ‌and ​his ​property.
- ‌**The ‌Cackler** — ‌His ​sacred ​goose ‌gives ​him the ​epithet ‌“the ​Cackler”; ​his ‌cry was ​the ‌world’s ​first ​sound ​in some ​cosmogonies.
- ‌**Father ‌of ​the ‌Ennead** — ​By ​Nut ‌he ‌fathered ‌Osiris, ‌Isis, Seth, ​Nephthys, ‌Horus ​the ​Elder ​— the ‌gods ​whose ​quarrels ​drive ‌Egyptian myth.
- ​**Judge ​of ​the ‌Divine ​Tribunal** — ‌He ​presides ‌over ​the ‌council of ‌gods ​in ​the ​succession ​myth of ‌Horus ‌and ​Seth.

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Geb as father and throne-estate).

mythology.body:
Geb’s mythology ​is the deep structure ‌under the Osiris cycle: ‌the separation of ​earth and sky that ​creates the world’s ​space, and the divine ​tribunal over which he ​presides when Horus ‌and Seth dispute the ​succession. His jealousy of ​Osiris — in ‌one strand he lies ​with Nut and ‌fathers the five gods ​on the forbidden days ‌— is the ​genealogical knot of the ​whole pantheon.[^1]

### Parted from ​Nut (Heliopolitan Cosmogony)

​Born of Shu and ​Tefnut, Geb and ‌Nut loved without space ​between them until Shu, ‌on Ra’s command, ​wrenched them apart — ‌and the world’s breathable ​distance dates from ‌that separation. Geb’s green ​fertility and Nut’s ‌starry vault remain arched ​apart for eternity, the ​air god’s arms ‌the only thing between ‌them.[^2]

### The Five Children ‌on the Epagomenal ​Days (Pyramid Texts)

Though ​the birth of ‌the five gods belongs ​to Nut’s myth, the ​Pyramid Texts address ‌Geb as their father ​and as the mountain ​of the west ‌on which the dead ​king ascends. ‘You ‌are Geb, the heir ​of the gods,’ the ​utterances tell the ​king — the earth ​is the ultimate estate ‌of succession.

### The ‌Tribunal of Geb (Contendings ​of Horus and ‌Seth)

In the New ​Kingdom narrative of the ​divine lawsuit, the ‌gods weary of the ‌eighty-year dispute between Horus ‌and Seth and ‌appeal to Geb, who ​as earth and ‌eldest remaining power hears ​the case and awards ​the Two Lands ​to Horus, assigning Seth ‌to the desert and ​the thunder — ​the judicial myth behind ​the division of ‌the living king from ​the dangerous margins.

### The ​Earth Receives the ​Dead (Book of the ‌Dead)

Spell 125’s negative ​confession addresses the ‌earth directly — ‘I ​have not polluted ‌the soil’ — because ​the soil is Geb’s ‌body and the ‌dead enter it as ​guests. The grave itself, ​the shaft and ​chamber, is a doorway ​into the god; ‌to be buried was ‌literally to be taken ​into Geb.

hieroglyphic-evidence.body:
The name Gb is written in Egyptian hieroglyphs as a theonym with the divine determinative. Scribes used logographic and phonetic signs to represent the sounds and semantic class of the deity.

The restoration Gb transliterates Egyptological convention, preserving the distinction between sign function and phonetic value.[^1]

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Geb as father and throne-estate).

pyramid-texts.body:
The Pyramid Texts, inscribed in royal tombs of the Old Kingdom, contain the earliest references to Gb. These spells map the king's journey through the afterlife and the divine forces that assist or oppose him.

The restored name Gb reflects scholarly transliteration of those hieroglyphic spells.[^1]

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Geb as father and throne-estate).

coffin-texts.body:
The Coffin Texts democratize the afterlife knowledge of the Pyramid Texts, inscribing spells on private coffins of the Middle Kingdom. Gb appears in mortuary and cosmological passages that protect the deceased.

The Unicode restoration Gb continues the Egyptological reading of those texts.[^1]

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Geb as father and throne-estate).

book-of-the-dead.body:
The Book of the Dead, a New Kingdom compilation of spells, includes references and imagery connected with Gb. Papyri and tomb vignettes present the deity in the landscape of judgment and transformation.

The restored spelling Gb preserves the scholarly form used in modern editions.[^1]

sources.citation: Pyramid Texts (Geb as father and throne-estate).
